tool.measures: the inclusions, texture and purity of the stone, at high magnification

steps.title: Seeing inside a stone
steps.text: The 10× loupe already shows a lot, but the microscope goes further: it magnifies 10 to 60 times and lights the stone so that you look inside. What you look for there are the inclusions: small foreign bodies, cavities or cracks trapped in the stone. They tell how it formed.

steps.title: Magnification and focus
steps.text: The more you magnify, the finer you see, but the thinner the sharp zone is. At high magnification, only a very thin slice of the stone is sharp: you turn the wheel to go from one slice to another. The ×60 objective (the strongest) shows the finest inclusions, but the focus must be precise.

steps.title: Inclusions and their story
steps.text: • Fine, parallel needles (the “silk”): typical of natural ruby and sapphire. • A garden of cracks and small crystals: natural emerald. • Round bubbles and curved trails: a glass or a flame-fusion synthetic. • Whole crystals (a small zircon, a garnet): proof of a stone born in the earth. A stone with no inclusion at all is not necessarily synthetic, but a stone without a flaw deserves some doubt.

steps.title: Natural or synthetic?
steps.text: Inclusions help tell a stone from nature from a made one: • synthetics often have curved growth lines (Verneuil method) or veils and remains of flux; • natural stones show irregular crystals and cracks. It is a clue, never proof on its own: it is cross-checked with the other instruments.

steps.title: Rough stone: the window
steps.text: A rough stone has a rough surface that scatters light: you see nothing. In the lapidary workshop, the window polisher polishes a small flat facet. Through this window, you look inside under the microscope and judge the clarity before deciding to cut. The camera of the microscope then takes a picture of what you see, to attach to the report.

steps.title: To remember
steps.text: • The microscope is mainly used to see inclusions. • You raise the magnification little by little and sweep the stone with the wheel. • Inclusions show the nature of the stone, sometimes its deposit and its treatments (filled cracks, laser holes). • The result is cross-checked with the other instruments.
